beats.prose: Floating comes down to density, mass packed into a given volume. Anything less dense than the liquid it sits in will float, and anything denser will sink. Ice floats because it is roughly nine percent less dense than the liquid water beneath it, so the real question is not why ice floats but why freezing makes water less dense in the first place.

beats.prose: In liquid water, molecules tumble over one another in loose, ever-shifting clusters. Hydrogen bonds form and break constantly, letting molecules pack fairly close together as they move. That constant rearranging is what keeps liquid water relatively dense: there is not much wasted space between molecules at any given instant.

beats.prose: As water freezes, the molecules stop tumbling and lock into a fixed hexagonal lattice, each one hydrogen-bonded to four neighbors at a specific angle. That angle forces open, six-sided channels through the structure, like scaffolding built from hexagons instead of a tight stack of bricks. The rigid geometry that makes ice strong is the same geometry that makes it spacious.
beats.note: The hexagonal lattice is also why snowflakes are six-sided.

beats.prose: Spacious means fewer molecules fit into the same volume, so the same mass of water takes up more room as ice than as liquid. Density is mass divided by volume, and when the volume goes up while the mass stays fixed, density has to go down. That is the whole mechanism: freezing does not add molecules, it just spreads the same ones into a wider lattice.

beats.prose: It is tempting to think ice floats simply because it is cold, as if temperature itself controls floating. But cold water sinks, not floats, right up until it actually turns to ice. What matters is not temperature directly but the structural change at the freezing point, when molecules snap into that open lattice.

figure.caption: Liquid water is densest at about 4°C, not at its freezing point.

beats.prose: Above 4°C, water behaves as expected: warmer means more motion, more spreading out, lower density. But between 4°C and 0°C, water starts pre-forming small, short-lived patches of that open ice-like structure while still liquid, which lowers density slightly instead of raising it. The result is a density peak at 4°C, with cooler water floating above it and ice floating above all of it.

beats.prose: This ordering has a real consequence: ice forms at the surface of lakes and oceans first, insulating the liquid water below rather than sinking and freezing a body of water solid from the bottom up. Fish and other aquatic life survive winters because of this quirk in how water's molecules pack themselves.
